title: Passing messages with queues

spans.text: Goal: apply “Passing messages with queues” to a real program or device. The key principle is: A queue gives a clearer ownership and synchronization boundary than an unprotected global. In a project, follow this guidance: Size the queue for bursts and consumer rate, and define what happens when it fills.
QUESTION: What will this example do? Predict the result first.
Serial Monitor prints incrementing integers produced by one task and consumed by another.
A queue stores fixed-size items in FIFO order and decouples producer and consumer tasks.
can block with a timeout; payloads are copied, so large objects need deliberate pointer-lifetime management. Check the send result instead of silently losing data when a queue is full.
void producer(void*) { int value = 0; for (;;) { ++value; if (xQueueSend(readings, &value, pdMS_TO_TICKS(100)) != pdPASS) vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(100)); vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(500)); } }

What it does: A queue gives a clearer ownership and synchronization boundary than an unprotected global.
Why it is used: Size the queue for bursts and consumer rate, and define what happens when it fills.
If omitted or changed: Check that queue creation succeeded; larger queues consume more RAM.
